entries.name: Reproductive Coercion

approved_draft.why_this_matters: A decision that belongs to one person's body and life ends up made under the weight of what refusal would cost them — job, money, support, standing in the family.
approved_draft.what_it_is_not: People are allowed to want things and say so: a parent hoping for grandchildren, a partner describing the family they imagined. A neutral, lawful employment policy can also touch a reproductive decision without targeting it. What changes the picture is a consequence attached to the answer.

existing_specific_text.short_definition: Controlling reproductive choices through institutional pressure, career consequences, or elimination of support.
existing_specific_text.expanded_definition: Controlling another person's reproductive choices — whether to have children, when, or how many — through institutional pressure, career consequences, financial leverage, or the withdrawal of support, rather than respecting the choice as the individual's own to make. This can come from a partner, family, employer, or institution.

what_it_sounds_like: Career or financial consequences implied or applied based on a reproductive decision the target is considering or has made.
Support (financial, emotional, practical) made conditional on a reproductive choice going a particular way.
Pressure applied through repeated, escalating institutional or family channels rather than respecting a stated decision as final.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People often have genuine feelings and hopes about family planning that they share without any attached leverage. Neutral policies sometimes intersect with reproductive decisions without targeting them specifically.
common_false_positives: A genuine, one-time expression of a personal opinion or hope about family planning, offered without any attached leverage or consequence.
An employer's genuinely neutral, legally-compliant policy that happens to intersect with a reproductive decision, without targeting it.
Family members sharing real feelings about wanting grandchildren or similar, without any actual leverage attached to the sharing.

Is support genuinely conditional on the outcome, or does it continue regardless of what's decided?

Would a reasonable person see the pressure as an attempt to override the individual's own choice?
